items.title: Olivia Bee 2026
items.excerpt: We’ll jump right in. What’s changed since we last interviewed you, eight years ago? Easy one. So much! I live in rural america now, I run a farm with my husband. I’m married. I have a child. I feel like I grew up in the city not knowing that some things were an option. I never knew
items.content:
We’ll jump right in. What’s changed since we last interviewed you, eight years ago? Easy one.

So much! I live in rural america now, I run a farm with my husband. I’m married. I have a child.

I feel like I grew up in the city not knowing that some things were an option. I never knew that you could live in rural America or that you could have a horse. I just thought that was something you were born into and you couldn’t choose that. But, you know, there were always inklings of this kind of stuff when I was a little kid. We were always gardening and my parents had a big yard. We were always outside and I was always really interested in, say, the tomato that came from the garden. It’s all been  a road map back to myself. I feel like that’s especially evident when you have a kid, I’m remembering all these things that got me excited as a kid and seeing myself through new eyes. Coming back to myself in ways that maybe I didn’t expect but feel very natural.

Yeah, most importantly though, how goes the work? Babies are nice and all, but what about photography!

It’s good! I just want to make the most magical childhood for my daughter. And so that ends up being in pictures because I’m always photographing what I’m going through in my life and what’s happening, whether that’s an external circumstance or observation or an internal monologue or fantasy. I’ve been photographing our life on the farm, but with this new magical inclination. I’m being drawn to making costumes and making little houses out of papier-mâché, growing just like a shit ton of flowers so that my daughter can be in a field of flowers. My life comes first, my photographs come second, but my photographs are always evidence of that life, or proof. It comes from life first and it’s always been that way. So it’s good. I’m shooting more commercial work, which is really fun. I feel like I need it. It’s generative for me to go out and be creative for other people and get paid and go on a trip. To have to deal with all these challenges that come with shooting commercially and then bring that hustle back to my home and seeing things with a new set of eyes because I was just in a different setting. They inform each other.

How does the professional field feel for you? The last few years have been very tumultuous for people in photography.

There’s a lot to be afraid of. And I try not to go there, because then I can’t get out. With AI, you know, some people’s careers are just over, if you don’t pivot, it’s going to be gone. There’s this push, the world’s going in two different directions in terms of visuals, there’s the super-obvious, “perfect AI can do this, why wouldn’t we have AI do this?” Then there’s this whole real attraction to human imperfection. And I’ve always been attracted to human imperfection and how that makes things beautiful. So I’m diving into that even more. Because I don’t think that can be replaced with AI, I think AI is does a great job at, unfortunately, things like e-commerce, and which I think people should be still shooting as a job, I don’t think we need to save j crew, like, tons of money, and the thing I don’t get about AI is, do you not realize that if all the jobs of the people who buy your things are gone, you won’t be able to sell your shit. You need all those blue collar white collar people to buy your dumb t shirts.

It’s part of the ecosystem.

Yeah, exactly. They’re not thinking about that. They’re thinking about cutting their numbers, not like, where’s our consumer going to be? And you see people struggling to, I mean, obviously, gas right now. Just doing life is a lot more expensive than it used to be. But people seem to be paid less, across the board, not just in the photography industry, I think in general, no raises yet your taxes go up, gas is more expensive, groceries
are more, just everything’s more expensive. All that to say, I’m choosing to be optimistic. And that people will always want a human touch. And I feel like there’s always going to be doom and gloom. It’s pretty tense.

In our industry, you can always be like, “well, it wasn’t like the 80s. Well, it wasn’t like the early 2000s.” And so I try to think in terms of, okay, what in 20 years are people going to be like, “God, I wish I could go back to that. It wasn’t like it was in 2026.” Which sounds crazy to say out loud, but what are those avenues to develop in and try to pivot under? There’s still ad work, but it’s definitely different. I’m trying to go for things that I maybe I didn’t shoot when I was younger. I think it’s either adapt or migrate or die. So it’s hard staying where you are and wishing things were different, it’s hard changing and figuring out how to be present and current…you choose your hard.

Part of that too, is surrounding myself with positive people. People who recognize the difficulties in the industry, but want to keep going and want to
find the good in it. People are always going to need a human touch, people always going to want human stories, or at least the world I want to live in and the world I want for my daughter. And even if that world is maybe less than the whole world, I think it’s still going to be there.

Do you feel like you’ve got a balance right now between like your art and your life?

I feel like I have a balance between my art and my life but it’s an ever-evolving dance, especially with the seasonality of farm work. Admittedly, I’m not doing as much of the manual labor as I used to because I’m the primary caregiver and joe has to be on the tractor a lot, but I feel so lucky for Mary, too, because we’re both able to be home. She gets to be with us 24-7.

When you’re a mom you’ve become a little more efficient with your time or maybe inefficient in other ways, but like, “okay I have 15 minutes while she’s playing with blocks or asleep or is really into this book, I better make the most of this 15 minutes because I’m gonna want to be with her
after when she’s not focused on something else or if she’s not sleeping.” It’s a challenge. Commercial stuff is not usually on schedule. My schedule is based on her schedule and then hopefully other things fit into it or I have to figure it out. I’d like to be working more, I would love to be doing a shoot a month, I think i’m headed back to that. Everything’s how it’s supposed to be. Also, it’s so beautiful here right now, it’s like this every day for months so it’s not a bad time to be home…but I have a big job in two weeks. So I’m excited for that.

I used to be like, “I wish I could only do my personal work and not do any commercial work.” And I did that. And it really sucks to be a starving artist. It sucks. I wasn’t creative, because I was in survival mode, and I know a lot of people can relate to that. I was literally just thinking, “how are we going to make these next bill payments?” I’m not thinking, “oh, it’d be great if I turned into a butterfly today.” It gave me a lot of perspective, because when I started taking pictures, I was still a dependent of my parents, and I was working that way. I got to really explore what I wanted to say and how I wanted to shoot without the pressure of making money.

Why is it that you think your career has survived when other people seem to be floundering?

I don’t think it came without floundering, I’ve definitely had moments of floundering or thinking, “is this floundering?” or, “floundering is coming.” I’m definitely lucky, in a way. I’m always trying to…yeah, I’ll take a million pictures of myself in a field at sunset, but I am trying to do new things, too.

I don’t try to follow trends. I try to figure out what’s next for me and what’s interesting to me and hopefully that changes. I realized after Kids in Love and after I moved to rural America, “okay, I can’t be hired for kids having fun out in the world forever, because I’m not going to be a kid out in the world having fun forever.” I look at Rihanna, she’s evolved so many times. And she does stuff on her own timeline. I’m always thinking, “okay, what would Rihanna do? She’d probably do something different. She’d probably try something new, but still be herself.” And she’s so unapologetically herself, even when it’s new or different.

Are you still using large format right now?

Not really. It’s too expensive. I’m sure I will return to it. I was also craving something between large format and 35mm, so I’ve been shooting mostly medium format and trying to marry those two worlds. I wanted a quicker way of image-making. I had a self-timer I’d had made by this robotics company to take pictures with my large format…but they didn’t last that long. So then I was always asking Joe, “can you please help me take a picture??” He’s always willing, of course. But I got into taking self-portraits because of the autonomy. So self-timer is my best friend, mainly with a Mamiya, most of the time. I mean, I still sprinkle in 35mm, even if it’s just disposable cameras. I always have one in my bag, but mostly Mamiya.

How is it being married to another photographer?

Oh, it’s cool. Joe is the kind of artist that won’t make something for a year and then he’ll go and make the most beautiful picture and I’m
almost like, “fuck you. ” I have to be fully available and taking pictures all the time to keep that muscle alive and well and I feel like he can just turn it on and be like, “ah, I’m back.” But it’s great. We have a lot to talk about, photo-wise. We have the same interests, agriculture and photography,
but I would say he’s more interested in agriculture than I am, and I’m more interested in photography than he is, it’s a nice balance.

I love that he loves image-making and sometimes he makes these pictures that make me think, “oh my god, how did you even get that?” And he gets it so fast.  I’ve been told I’m a pretty fast shooter by many people and I’m like, “you have not seen my husband.” The gut feeling, he is so good at just trusting that and coming out of this quiet time I had in my working life is a return to trusting in that gut feeling. He reminds me a lot that that’s my most important asset.

Have your inspirations changed over the past few years?

Yeah, I would say the list has gotten shorter. I’m looking to the ground a lot more because my kid’s down there. And I’m noticing bugs. And really, I have a macro lens now that I love. And I was like, “why did I never have a macro lens? This is so fun, seeing the world so small.” Sometimes I just use it for a portrait, but you can see the pores on the skin and I just…I used to be really interested in the landscape of the body and sensuality. And now I’m really interested in the landscape of the close-up, the close-up of my daughter’s eyes or my hair on her face or
how the water drips off of her hair, small things like that.

Details.

Yeah, small details become the landscape. I was just so interested in the body in a landscape and the body becoming the landscape. And yeah, now it’s the details. It’s kind of the opposite of what Sally Mann talks about when her work, when she was shooting immediate family, and then she went into her landscape stuff, her children were still in the pictures, and then she kept zooming out. So it was way more the landscape than the pictures and than the children and the children disappeared all together, but I feel it’s the opposite for me. Maybe that’s because I became a mother much further into my photographic journey than she did.

I also I had a very close friend of mine die, a year and a half ago now. And she respected all living beings down to like, the dung beetle, you know, and so I’ve been more appreciative of that, while we while she was here with us, but also after she died.

Is there work you’re excited to make in the future?

Oh, I mean always. I’m making a film. So that is very exciting. It might take a minute, but I’m making a film. A full length.

You did a short about dog sled racing.

Yeah, I did a short about about mushing, a short doc. I did my narrative short about the dancer, I’ve done plenty of music videos and things but definitely always craved doing something longer, so I’m excited about that.

Is this one you’ve written yourself as well?

Currently writing, yeah. It’s always about personal experiences, but made a little bit more palatable.

How often are you taking pictures right now?

I take a picture every day, sometimes that’s on my phone, and maybe it’s not something I’m going to put in a gallery, but it’s still using my visual brain. I go out to take pictures once a week, maybe twice a week. It depends on the weather, I get really inspired when it’s so lush and green outside and there’s rainbows and sometimes it’s raining and sometimes sunny and there’s flowers. You can be outside, not wearing a coat and you can sit on the ground. So, I’ll probably be taking more pictures now and then sometimes in the winter, less.

Have you considered doing other shows, other books?

For sure. I had a show last summer and books are how I think about pictures, it’s always a chapter of a book, but it’s such a thing to get them published. I think a book is warranted, but there’s nothing in the works right now. I’m always shooting for the next show and the next book so there there will be one.

Do you see the chapters of your life clearly?

Absolutely. In the pictures and the way I was taking pictures, oh yeah.

How do you articulate those chapters to yourself?

In a chapter of your life, what are the things you’re returning to? There are usually common themes, like, birds were really speaking to me then and I always wore this dress or whatever. It can seem like a superficial thing, but I think about it like, okay, if there’s a character in a movie that’s always wearing a red dress and suddenly she’s wearing a green dress, you think, okay, there’s something happening there and I feel like it’s the same in my life. It can come through clothing, it can come through a certain camera and how that makes you look at things a little differently. I get married to a camera for five years and then I move on. I don’t have to articulate it visually, it just happens, it’s not something I have to think about too hard. There are the common themes that I always come back to, you know, the body and the landscape, connection between people, pink, eggs, life and death, etc.

When I think of your career, the chapters of your work, it feels very city-based for me, there’s the early Portland period, then there’s the New York period, then there’s the LA period and there’s the return to Oregon period.

Totally, I think that’s accurate. The pictures that don’t resonate with me anymore are, yeah, the LA and New York pictures. I just like the pictures I’ve taken in Oregon. I like some of them, and I like certain projects I did. I think it’s more…maybe I just didn’t like my life as much. I liked the projects I
would go shoot and seek out, but when I was documenting my everyday life, which is such a life force for me and my creativity. I mean, I had a nice life. I had a great life, but it wasn’t deeply inspiring to me. The professional work was inspiring.

There’s a reason you came back to Oregon. It was a journey for you, where you had to have these other adventures to come back to Oregon.

Absolutely. I think about it in terms of place as well, that’s an inherent change of scenery, and an indicator that something has changed because it’s very obvious something has changed!

And there there is no anticipating what the next chapter is going to be?

No, I can imagine, there’ll be more kids, we’ll definitely have one more. We might not stay in Oregon forever, we want to figure that out before Mary is school age.

Where would you want to go?

Probably Montana or Wyoming and have a more Western way of life. We don’t want to be chicken farming forever. Joe is a horse boy, he’s ridden horses his whole life. He’s a champion in endurance riding. We have his horse, we have my horse, but he doesn’t want to go trail ride anymore and we want to be working with animals.

What we have here is wonderful, there are amazing people, it’s close to a lot of amenities. I’m not ready to leave, yet, but I imagine a world where we’re more in the wild. We want to be ranching rather than farming. Yeah, we’ve got a little time. But it goes by really quick, really quick.

More horse photos is what you really want.

Yeah! More horse photos. I always wanted to have an artist retreat when I lived in Eastern Oregon. That was kind of the plan, but then COVID hit and the place wasn’t really big enough for that. Maybe I could host a workshop or two, or a dinner, but we really want to have a dedicated place for artist retreats and also maybe a ranching school, because agriculture is dying in the US. It’s getting so much worse and young people can’t afford it, including us. You know, we have good other jobs and it’s so expensive.

So thinking about something like that in the long term and also, I want a studio that’s separate from the house, we’re just thinking about things that would make a dream thing. And then also maybe some multi-generational living, probably closer to his family, because his parents are both retired and more available for helping with kids.

It seems like you have a lot of ideas that seem possible to you, as grim as things can be.

You have to think it’s possible or it won’t happen. Joe is a big dreamer and I’m a big dreamer who’s also a realist. We’ve had to meet each other in the middle, like, “okay, let’s dream, I can dream bigger but it also needs to be able to happen.” We’re crazy like that and also a good team, but I don’t think other people understand our decision-making, which is fine, only we need to understand our decision-making.

It’s all seemed to really come together.

It always does, maybe it takes a second, but it always does.

Yeah, you’ve always seemed both aspirational and grounded.

That’s the balance of living on a farm and working with my hands and also going to LA to go shoot Kesha or whatever it is. I need that sparkle, but also that rootedness and, honestly, that shit. I deal with poop every day. I need that, but also the sparkly diamond fantasy of whatever it is and where those things come to me. I feel so lucky to be able to live in that dance, but also, I worked hard to cultivate that dance and figure out how we were going to dance.

Where do you think that combination came from?

That’s a great question.

Thank you.

Ha! I feel like you just go through life and try stuff and figure out what works for you the best. Maybe that was pretty evident when I was living in New York. I moved to LA from New York because I never saw the sky in New York and I have to see the sky…but that party I was at last night was really cool. I loved both but I didn’t know how to have both. How to have both to me was working in New York and then going to Oregon for two weeks in the summer and going camping…but also going to house parties and farms. Now I live those principles instead of borrowing from those principles. Now that’s what my life is built around.

And do you think that your tendency to go for the things you want allowed you to get both of those things?

Of course. Yeah, of course. And I want Mary to know that she can have that too. Whatever she wants. I want her to figure out how to… in some dark periods in the last year and a half I’ve been like, “I have to figure this out because I need my daughter to be proud of me and to know that she can do that too.” I just want her to be able to flourish. I don’t want her to just survive. I want her to thrive. And how is she going to get there? I need
to show her that it’s possible.

items.title: In photos: Black Texas life since emancipation
items.excerpt: Kinship & Community — A new photobook and exhibition showcases the rich culture, history and community of African American folks in the Lone Star State, whose existence in the region predates colonial Britain. On J
items.content:
Kinship & Community — A new photobook and exhibition showcases the rich culture, history and community of African American folks in the Lone Star State, whose existence in the region predates colonial Britain.

On June 19, 1865 – some months after the Confederacy surrendered in ignominious defeat – Black folks in Texas were liberated from the bondage of chattel slavery. A year later, the first celebration of Jubilee Day (later Juneteenth) was held, the annual event to help people register to vote. During the first flush of Reconstruction, Black communities built Freedmen’s towns, forming the heart and soul of newly emerging cities like Houston with its fabled Third and Fourth Wards. 

By the 1870s, photography had democratised the portrait, wresting the power of representation from the powerbrokers and restoring it to the people themselves. Inexpensive image making techniques, such as tintypes and crayon portraits, became popular among Black folks on both sides of the camera. But it wasn’t until 1995, when writer and filmmaker Alan Govenar and artist Kaleta Doolin teamed up to create the Texas African American Photography Archive (TAAP) that this history could be told in full. Home to 60,000 images made between the 1850s and the 1970s in a broad array of formats, TAAP has become one of the foremost repositories of work by Black photographers in the world. 

With the new exhibition and book, Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive (Aperture/Documentary Arts), co-curators Nicole R. Fleetwood and Brian Wallis craft a panoramic landscape of everyday life as seen from the inside looking out. Featuring work by Earlie Hudnall Jr., Marion Butts, Elnora W. Frazier, Alonzo Jordan, and Benny A. Joseph, as well as a photographic essay by Rahim Fortune, and essay by Deborah Willis, Kinship & Community is a celebration of Black Texas in all its multi-splendored glory. 

  • Read next: ‘Hyper-American’ photos of life in rural Texas

“Texans are very proud of their history, but I think the rest of the country, and maybe even the world, has reduced and misread the history of Black Texas,” says Fleetwood, who has her own personal ties to the state. Hailing from a small town in Ohio, she moved to Houston briefly when her mother remarried but was completely overwhelmed. “I left after a year,” she says. “I didn’t understand the landscape of Texas.” 

But Fleetwood, who is now based in New York, has come full circle and has a place in Houston to which she regularly returns. She, like many of her generation, have embraced remigration, returning to the South and finding kinship and community among new arrivals from Nigeria and Black Americans who never left. Personal engagement is a hallmark of Fleetwood’s work, from her landmark 2020 exhibition and book, Marking Time: Art in the Age of Mass Incarceration, to her forthcoming memoir, Between the River and the Railroad Tracks. 

  • Read next: A visual journey through Texas during lockdown

Seen through the lens of TAAP, the rich cultural histories of Black Texas form a majestic tapestry of everyday life. Fleetwood points to the cowboy, originally a radicalised term used to diminish the contributions of Black cowhands, as well as the presence of Black communities that predate Jamestown, the first British settlement on the continent. “The earliest African presence in Texas were people who [were brought by Spanish colonisers] before the formation of the US as a nation state, and many of them were early settlers in rural parts of Texas,” she says. 

With roots that run deeper than the nation itself, Black Texas is the cornerstone of America. “The sense of pride in Texas is unlike any other state,” Fleetwood says. “One of my brothers was born there and he is so Texan. He lives in a community in Houston called Hiram Park, and it’s home to Black cowboys that Rahim Fortune has been documenting. If you’re hanging out in my brother’s yard, you’ll see five or 10 guys riding their horses and playing music. They’re somewhat country, somewhat hip hop, and it just blows my mind.’”

  • Read next: Rahim Fortune’s dreamlike vision of the Black American South

Kinship & Community: Selections from the Texas African American Photography Archive and Rahim Fortune - Between a Memory and Me: A Photographic Essay are on view through September 5, 2026, at Art + Practice in collaboration with the California African Art Museum in Los Angeles. Kinship & Community is published by Aperture/Documentary Arts.

items.title: Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time
items.content:
Damien Aubin Documents a Former Soviet Mining Settlement Suspended in Time

July 24, 2026
BooksHistoryPhotography
Grace Ebert
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

The small settlement of Pyramiden on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard is literally frozen in time. A former mining outpost for the Soviet Union, industrial operations ceased in 1998, and residents relocated. It wasn’t until 2007 that a handful of new inhabitants made the settlement home.

Because Pyramiden was abandoned in a cold climate, it remains impeccably preserved, with remnants of its once-thriving settlement still visible. French photographer Damien Aubin visited the Arctic region and documented the still, serene environment blanketed in snow. “The place has not been abandoned. It has been left in suspension,” he says.

Pyramiden’s buildings and the objects inside are largely unchanged. Books sit open on school desks, and an unblemished statue of Lenin presides over a common area. Outside, a towering outdoor monument soars into the sky, the vibrant red and blue paint a stark contrast to the otherwise white landscape.

“I photograph these environments at a distance, in a restrained, diffuse light. There is no event to describe, no narrative to unfold,” Aubin adds. “Across Pyramiden, Barentsburg and Longyearbyen, the same condition appears:
spaces shaped by human intent, no longer aligned with it.”

Aubin has compiled the photos in a limited-edition book slated for release in September. You can purchase a copy on his website.

items.title: Youthful joy & end-of-era poignancy at a London school prom
items.excerpt: Leavers — For several years, Lewis Khan documented young people as they celebrated the last of their school days and the completion of their exams. The series is now collated in a new self-published photobook and short film.
items.content:
Leavers — For several years, Lewis Khan documented young people as they celebrated the last of their school days and the completion of their exams. The series is now collated in a new self-published photobook and short film.

The protagonists of Lewis Khan’s Leavers revel in a cloak of youth-shaped exuberance. Draped in sequins and silk or adorned with a bowtie and sunglasses – one teenager wears a sash pronouncing him ‘Prom King’, others don the traditional dress of their home lives – these young people appear confident, oftentimes euphoric and occasionally serious (but ultimately comfortable), embracing the kind of party atmosphere uniquely fuelled by exams being over. A soft glow, courtesy of the photographer’s preferred use of medium format and Super 8, underscores the gravity of the moment, between the end of school and what comes next. “It’s a moment of joy and celebration,” reflects Khan. 

The near-decade long project first took shape, loosely, in July 2017 when the photographer accompanied his mum on a night time stroll around their neighbourhood in Vauxhall, south London. It was the type of local walk that doesn’t entertain any real objective, recalls Khan, “No direction, just soaking things up.” At some point they noticed groups of teenagers spilling out of a nearby school: their shiny suits and glittering frocks generating a spectacle in an otherwise grey landscape of concrete and traffic. His interest piqued, Khan reached out to the school via a friend’s mum who taught there, and arranged to shoot the following year’s event.

Despite its popularity in the UK growing substantially in the past few decades, prom remains largely an American phenomenon for many, witnessed predominantly through TV and film, where the lead characters are generally white and typically depicted as middle or upper middle class. Khan, who grew up in the area, doesn’t recall his own secondary school ever hosting a prom. “I don’t think it had the resources,” he says. “I would have gone to it though. And if my old school ever does do a prom, I would love to photograph it.” In his work however, there’s a sense of familiarity about the occasion; a recognisable intimacy that betrays the specificity of the scene. Now, following an exhibition at 1014 gallery in Dalston earlier this year, the photographer has self-published a book of his prom pictures. 

  • Read next: Inside the bedrooms of American youth during the ’80s and ’90s

Beyond the project’s strong visual component, there’s an important social factor and a cultural significance that Khan observed early on, which quickly became a central motivation for returning every year. “I’ve grown up knowing teenagers to be treated with suspicion and contempt,” he shares, referencing the ASBO era. Entering his teens in the early 2000s, the photographer remembers well the controversy of anti-social behaviour orders, which arrived with Tony Blair’s Labour government in 1998 – introduced as part of the Crime and Disorder Act – and how they coincided with a culture of councils rescinding resources like youth clubs for teenagers. “At the same time, they were installing high frequency audio signals in public places that only younger people could hear, making those spaces inhospitable.

“It created this sense that young people weren’t to be supported or understood, but managed and moved on,” he continues. “Those attitudes were often mapped onto existing social and racial inequalities, which you can see reflected in patterns of systemic racism, for example police stop and search figures in areas like Lambeth [where the school is], which disproportionately affect Black boys and men.” Leavers then, becomes a counternarrative, challenging negative stereotypes perpetuated by biased newspaper headlines. As Khan observes, “The prom felt like a beautiful antidote. A space of self-worth and pride.” 

In his photographs, made with a pronounced sense of care, Khan reframes both what a prom can look like and how teenagers from inner-city London state schools are perceived; the scenes are joyful and the environment feels kind, as friends and classmates dance, joke, and encourage one another. There is a sense that judgement – both the sort presented in classic teen movies with high-stakes proms, and the kind found in ‘only three school children at a time’ signs in London corner shops – has been removed for a night.

  • Read next: Unseen portraits of high school teenagers in ’70s New York

This sentiment is amplified in an accompanying short film, made in 2022, which features a specially-written poem by former Young People’s Laureate Caleb Femi, who grew up in Peckham in the neighbouring borough of Southwark. With Glass, which Femi recites alongside Lara George’s ‘Dansaki’, his words affect a kinship with the young people in Khan’s images, further sharpening the context in which they celebrate and the significance of their coming together; elsewhere a teacher makes this feeling explicit, tenderly announcing: “The most important thing is, through it all, you have made it to today. Whatever you went through – whatever you didn’t go through – somehow you are here today, and that is a celebration.”

Prior to Khan’s Dalston show, which marked his first solo exhibition, in spring last year Khan presented Leavers at photo festival Peckham24, while in September it travelled to Poland as part of Night of Photography with the Museum of Warsaw. “The response has been really generous,” he says today. “What’s stood out is how people connect – in Peckham there’s a familiarity with it being local, but even in places like Poland people still relate through their own memories of youth and moments of transition. That’s probably been the biggest surprise – how universal those feelings are, despite the work being so rooted in a specific place.”

  • Read next: “A party is a microcosm of a nation”: Caleb Femi on the decline of the house party

Leavers by Lewis Khan is available to purchase via his official website.

items.title: A High-Definition Cinematic Video Relives NASA’s Artemis II Mission
items.content:
A High-Definition Cinematic Video Relives NASA’s Artemis II Mission

July 20, 2026
FilmPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Between April 1 and 10 of this year, NASA’s Artemis II mission made history as four astronauts flew farther from Earth than anyone has ever traveled before. With state-of-the-art technology and numerous cameras onboard, the crew captured some of the most striking images we’ve seen of our planet as the flight path led them around our iconic satellite. Lenses attached to the exterior of the spacecraft, plus numerous photographers stationed on the ground during the launch, documented the literally out-of-the-this world process of rocketing through the planet’s atmosphere and keeping course around the moon.

John D. Boswell, a musician and filmmaker who works as MELODYSHEEP, created a cinematic short film compiled from videos and images published by NASA. His original music accompanies the public domain images and soundbites, providing a uniquely immersive glimpse of the historic mission. See more of his work on his Vimeo and YouTube channels.

items.title: ‘Voices in the Mirror’ Honors the Legacy of Pioneering Photographer Gordon Parks
items.content:
‘Voices in the Mirror’ Honors the Legacy of Pioneering Photographer Gordon Parks

July 17, 2026
PhotographySocial Issues
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

From portraits taken around Harlem in the 1940s to assignments for Life magazine to the 1963 March on Washington, Gordon Parks (1912-2006) wielded his camera as a tool for social justice. He captured civil rights activists like Malcom X and Martin Luther King, Jr. in addition to artists and celebrities such as Helen Frankenthaler and Ingrid Bergman. But he may be best known for his candid portraits of families and communities in the segregated South during the era of Jim Crow. All of these and more will be on view in Voices in the Mirror at Jack Shainman Gallery in mid-September, also marking the 20th anniversary of The Gordon Parks Foundation.

Parks was spurred to pursue photography in 1937 after seeing photos taken for the Farm Security Administration (FSA), which held a mission to document American life. “I saw that the camera could be a weapon against poverty, against racism, against all sorts of social wrongs,” he said. “I knew at that point I had to have a camera.” In 1942, he became the first Black photographer hired as part of the initiative, introducing him to Washington, D.C., where he noted that “discrimination and bigotry were worse there than any place I had yet seen.”

Among the images included in Voices in the Mirror are seminal portraits like “American Gothic, Washington, D.C.” (1942), which captures a government worker named Ella Watson with a broom and mop. The work nods to American Regionalist painter Grant Wood’s likewise iconic “American Gothic” painting, created 12 years earlier as an ode to American values. Parks’ image represented a starkly contrasted reality.

After speaking with Watson about her life and experience in D.C., Parks recalled that it was “so disastrous that I felt that I must photograph this woman in a way that would make me feel—or make the public feel—about what Washington, D.C., was in 1942.” He positioned her in front of a flag with a symbolic mop and broom. “I didn’t care about what anybody else felt,” he said. “That’s what I felt about America and Ella Watson’s position inside America.”

The exhibition is accompanied by numerous anecdotes and reflections by some of those who appeared in the photos or had close relationships with those who did, such as Malcolm X’s daughter, Qubilah Shabazz, and Cora Taylor, who was one of the women standing near a pair of segregated water fountains in “Segregation in the South” (1956).

Voices in the Mirror opens on September 18 and continues through November 7 in New York. You might also be interested in the works of other FSA photographers who documented the South during the 1930s and 1940s, such as Russell Lee and Marion Post Wolcott.

items.title: See Peter Marlow’s ‘The English Cathedral’ at London’s Oldest Gothic Church
items.content:
See Peter Marlow’s ‘The English Cathedral’ at London’s Oldest Gothic Church

July 15, 2026
HistoryPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Acclaimed British photographer Peter Marlow (1952-2016) was known for his journalistic attention to people and happenings in conflict zones and political interactions. Throughout his career, though, he also embarked on numerous personal documentary projects like Liverpool: Looking Out to Sea, which he completed in the late 1980s and early 1990s as the city experienced sharp economic decline—its historic docks were no longer viable for global industry. He was also president of Magnum Photos twice.

One of Marlow’s more meditative projects revolved around 42 Anglican cathedrals across England. The Anglican Christian tradition stems from the establishment of the Church of England following the English Reformation in the 16th century, although the cathedrals’ architectural lineage usually predates this period.

Completing The English Cathedral involved coordinating visits at times of day when Marlow could experience the buildings in natural light, not unlike the way they were seen for centuries before the advent of electricity. He focused on the churches’ naves, illuminating their rosette-covered wooden ceilings, Gothic arches, altars, and hints of apses beyond.

An exhibition of The English Cathedral opens on July 21 and continues through August 31 at Southwark Cathedral, which has roots dating back at least to the 11th century. Today, it’s the oldest Gothic church in London.

items.title: Experience Ana Mendieta’s Visceral, ‘Neolithic’ Work in a Major Survey
items.content:
Experience Ana Mendieta’s Visceral, ‘Neolithic’ Work in a Major Survey

July 15, 2026
ArtNaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Rarely do artists conceive of work that is prescient and, decades on, more urgent than when it was created. One who has accomplished this is certainly Ana Mendieta (1948-1985), whose interdisciplinary practice merged photography, land art, sculpture, film, and more. And in a large-scale, immersive survey of her work that opens today at Tate Modern, more than 120 pieces revisit the groundbreaking artist’s key series and empathetic exchange with land and nature.

Mendieta is best known for her Silueta Series, in which she impressed the shape of the human body in water, mud, rock, and forests. These sometimes consisted of outlines “drawn” onto surfaces, such as a gunpowder tribute on a fallen tree, which exists eternally half-ablaze in a photograph. Others are impressed directly into the earth, as if a person had been lying there for millennia as the desert or stone formed around her.

In what she described as “earth-body” works, Mendieta explored vital relationships between humans and nature, absence and presence, experience and temporality, and place and identity. She often turned the lens on herself, building compositions that plumb the tensions between beauty, ruggedness, vulnerability, and strength. Her practice can easily be viewed through the lens of ecofeminism, a movement that emerged around the same time Mendieta was working, but it is also profoundly personal.

At 12 years old, Mendieta was separated from her parents and brother, who remained in her home country of Cuba, when she and her sister were exiled to the U.S. following the Cuban Revolution in 1959. Throughout her life and brief career, she grappled with themes of displacement and disconnection. “My art is the way I reestablish the bonds that unite me to the Universe,” Mendieta said. “It is a return to the maternal source.”

There is also humor in her approach to self-representation, such as her early series of self-portraits in which she documented her wet hair in wild, sculptural forms or produced a sequential series of images in which an arrangement of flowers gradually conceals her face. Within a few years, the work adopted a more solemn, enigmatic tone, characterized by voids, organic forms, gesture, and ephemerality.

Mendieta also drew on her fascination with archaeology to create multimedia works that delved into the relationship between humans and the land. “My work is basically in the tradition of a Neolithic art,” she said in 1984. “I’m not interested in the formal qualities of my materials, but their emotional and sensual ones.”

The artist’s interest in the ancient past ultimately lends a timelessness to themes that resonate through her personal narrative but also, incidentally, the ills of the present. One might think of our screen-fueled social discord and the accelerating climate crisis, both also defined by a sense of alienation and disjointedness. Though Mendieta couldn’t have conceived of these things as we experience them today, she nevertheless tapped into a kind of visceral biophilia that’s more critical than ever. The exhibition at Tate highlights not only the artist’s the desire to connect with nature but also casts a light on how far removed from it most of us have become.

Ana Mendieta continues through January 17, 2027, in London. Plan your visit on Tate’s website.

items.title: A Documentary Journey in Cappadocia
International Aerial Photographer of the Year Contest Highlights the World from Above
items.content:
International Aerial Photographer of the Year Contest Highlights the World from Above

July 9, 2026
NaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

For a structure that was completed nearly 90 years ago, San Francisco’s Golden Gate Bridge possesses a kind of timeless modernity. It’s been the subject of countless photographs, often seen in the background from Baker Beach or from the overlook in Marin County. Its towers rise 500 feet from the roadway, but we typically can only see the structures from that level. For photographer Marcin Zając, a drone’s-eye view revealed a unique perspective of this iconic landmark.

Zając’s image is one of 101 finalists in the 2026 International Aerial Photographer of the Year, marking the second year of the competition. Photographers around the world submitted nearly 1,600 entries, with the top honor awarded to Azim Khan Ronnie, who draws on his background in journalism to capture human activities like fishing and harvesting crops.

Photographs considered for the competition range from drone views to shots taken from airplanes or the tops of buildings. Subject matter ranges from erupting volcanoes and geological phenomena to architecture and cultural events. See the top 101 photos on the contest’s website.

items.title: Rob Hann’s Chromatic and Quirky Landscapes Evoke Long-Distance Road Trips
items.content:
Rob Hann’s Chromatic and Quirky Landscapes Evoke Long-Distance Road Trips

July 9, 2026
Photography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

For more than three decades, Rob Hann has pursued the inimitable and notable, turning his lens toward public figures like Tom Hanks, David Byrne, Chloe Sevigny, Ray Lotta, Willem Dafoe, and many others. He also ranges across the breadth and length of the U.S., traversing storied highways like U.S. 89 in Arizona, a popular route to the Grand Canyon, or U.S. 90 in Texas, which passes through the artistic enclave of Marfa. Not unlike the way he captures portraits of people, his characterizations of the country’s endearingly quirky and remote places highlight individuality, presence, and the passage of time.

Hann’s subjects range from handmade road signs and vintage buildings to peculiar local attractions like trees completely covered in shoes. He sometimes captures site-specific artworks such as Nancy Holt’s “Sun Tunnels” (1973-76) in Utah’s Great Basin Desert or Magda Sayeg’s crocheted retro camper trailer at El Cosmico in Marfa. There’s often a tinge of tongue-in-cheek humor, too, such as a sign reading “ICY” amid an arid desert landscape in southeastern California or a half-buried car.

“Although my photos are usually very simple, I often like it when the viewer is not quite sure what it is that they’re seeing, when they have questions,” Hann tells Colossal. “I’m often attracted to things that are amusing, unintentionally funny, or things that are puzzling.”

For the vast majority of his career, Hann has shot with an analog Mamiya 7, only recently adding a digital camera to his routine: a Hasselblad X2D. One of the major differences is that the Mamiya takes a roll of film with only 10 frames, so there’s a more disciplined approach to avoid wasting rolls. With digital cameras, the number of images is only limited by the space on an SD card. “I try to make good decisions as I shoot and avoid wading through huge amounts of images on my computer when I get home,” Hann says. “With both cameras, I only use one fixed lens, and when shooting film, I just use one film stock.”

Color images have also emerged as an important tenet of Hann’s practice despite an earlier preference for black-and-white photography. “I was required to also shoot colour when working for magazines and record companies,” he says. “I could do it but struggled to make the colour photos special or make them feel like my own. It took me many years to get my head around making consistently good colour images.” Today, the emotive potential of color, explored through different levels of saturation and warmth, plays a significant role.

Hann is currently working with The Artist Edition toward the publication of a new book titled Wonder Valley, which is slated for release sometime later this year. Follow updates on Instagram.

items.title: Atmospheric Scenes and Layered Interpretations Top the 2026 Hasselblad Masters Contest
items.content:
Atmospheric Scenes and Layered Interpretations Top the 2026 Hasselblad Masters Contest

July 8, 2026
NaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In Pioche, Nevada, a movie theater built in 1937 stands in tribute to the immense changes in technology and style over nearly a century. A bold portrait set against a black background by photographer Kevin Boyle captures not only the aging building but a mid-20th-century pastime that taps into nostalgia and small town identity. (Amid preservation efforts, the theater is currently being rehabilitated.) It’s just one of the works in the artist’s ongoing Movieland series, which won the Architecture category in this year’s Hasselblad Masters 2026 contest.

Additional categories in the prestigious competition include Wildlife, Landscape, Art, Portrait, Street, and Project//21, which highlights work by entrants aged 21 or younger. This year, photographers in 160 countries submitted more than 108,000 images, which were narrowed down to 70 finalists.

In addition to their technical aptitude, the artists illuminate lesser-known pockets of the world by examining distinctive social issues, nature, and geographies. The winning photos are atmospheric and even surreal, such as Rohan Reilly’s low-exposure Ephemeral Visions series of rows of trees and Gosse Bouma’s misty depictions of Netherlandish market stalls in Morning Ritual.

Svetlana Jovanovic turns her lens to bold dual portraits of identical twins, and Alfred Minnaar’s otherworldly captures of underwater vitality topped the Wildlife category. Panitbhand Paribatra Na Ayudhya, winner of the Project//21 category, is a 14-year-old scuba diver from Thailand who explores the beauty, fragility, and biodiversity of the ocean in beautiful portrayals of marine life.

Hasselblad Foundation executive director Kalle Sanner says, “Across categories, the strongest work operated on more than one level simultaneously: legible on first encounter, yet resistant to easy interpretation. These are images that require attention, that continue to unfold the longer you stay with them.” For example, Yudha Kusuma Putera’s uncanny photographs of huddled cows’ backs nod to the unseen. What we don’t see is as significant as what we do, as these animals are actually grazing on heaps of trash in a dump on the outskirts of Yogyakarta, Indonesia. Exploring notions of labor and visibility, Putera takes a visually literal approach to “out of sight, out of mind.”

See all the winning images on the Hasselblad Masters website.

Katherine Wolkoff Meditates on Absence in Her Tender Photos of Deer Beds
items.content:
Katherine Wolkoff Meditates on Absence in Her Tender Photos of Deer Beds

July 2, 2026
ArtNaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

The last few mornings, as I’ve walked with my dog up the ravine behind my house, two fawns seem to bound of thin air, racing in unison through the trees until far enough way that they stop, stare, and wait for us to pass. It’s not uncommon to see several does grazing in the same woods, and I’ve always wondered where they sleep. Photographer Katherine Wolkoff followed a similar curiosity as she traversed the grassy meadows of Block Island, which sits a few miles off the coast of Rhode Island, for her series Deer Beds.

Flattened by lean cervid bodies, tall grasses reveal the areas where deer bed down. They don’t typically sleep in the same place every single night, but a home range area may have several spots that they return to repeatedly. Wolkoff prints the images at nearly life size, focusing directly on the nest-like spaces in intimate, horizonless meditations on comfort, presence, care, and resilience.

When the series was first exhibited, critic Eva Diaz noted in Artforum that “The prevailing metaphor of photography is that of the hunt. Photographers shoot, even stalk, their subjects; in the case of Katherine Wolkoff’s work, the absence of ‘prey’ itself becomes the subject of the project.” Sometimes during a walk, the artist encounters deer nestled in the grass and they dart away, startled. Other times, the beds are already empty.

“My mother, a science teacher, first mentioned deer beds to me, and I began walking the fields, following deer paths to find them,” Wolkoff tells Colossal. “That solitary, meditative search is still central to how I work today.” Broadly, her work focuses on the natural world in the Anthropocene, plumbing the relationship between humans and the land in light of the ongoing climate crisis.

The artist is currently finishing a book of pinhole photographs taken from the perspective of migrating birds on Block Island. “The resulting pictures have a blurred, frantic quality that I think of as visualizing the birds’ depletion: the chaos of an animal pushed to its limits over open water and unfamiliar coastline, flying through the night with no guarantee of where it will land or whether it will survive the crossing,” she says. Some of these works will be part of a forthcoming exhibition centered around the Atlantic Flyway at Benrubi Gallery next spring.

items.title: Theo Bosboom Takes a Bug’s-Eye View in His Perspective-Shifting ‘Flowerscapes’
items.content:
Theo Bosboom Takes a Bug’s-Eye View in His Perspective-Shifting ‘Flowerscapes’

July 1, 2026
NaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Stand in any forest and look up, and it’s hard not to be mesmerized by the swaying of tall trees and their elegant canopies casting shade onto the woodland floor. But imagine being an ant or beetle and peering up at the stems of wild geraniums, garlic, or buttercups and experiencing the same sensation. For photographer Theo Bosboom, this ground-level view of flowers and plants gave rise to a series that captures them in the way we might photograph a grove of towering, ancient sequoias.

Traversing local landscapes around his home in the Netherlands and sometimes venturing across the border into Germany or Belgium, Bosboom explores forests, dunes, public parks, roadside verges, and virtually any place that flowers grow. These excursions also sparked concern at the lack of pollinators he found among the flowers. “At times, it was eerily quiet,” he shares in the preface for his book, Flowerscapes, A Bug’s Eye View. “This matches recent studies showing that the numbers of flowers and insects have declined sharply across Western Europe over the past decades.”

There are a lot of reasons for the steep drop in insect populations, not just in Europe but around the world. Most of the reasons stem from human activities such as agriculture, pesticides, urban development and habitat destruction, pollution, and changing temperatures as a result of the escalating climate crisis.

Bosboom finds reasons to hope, however. He has observed how the Netherlands has adopted more environmentally friendly road management practices, and how people are becoming increasingly aware of the importance of native plants and wildflowers in supporting not only insect populations but entire ecosystems.

The diversity and resilience of flowers really struck a chord with Bosboom, who says, “The endlessly surprising perspectives completely captivated me, and I found myself constantly marvelling at their beauty, elegance, and strength.” He was also drawn to reducing his environmental impact by working more locally, sticking to destinations he could reach on foot or by bike or with just a short drive.

Purchase Flowerscapes, A Bug’s Eye View on Bosboom’s web shop, where you can also purchase prints, and explore much more of his work on Instagram.

items.title: United States of America: 250 Years
Scan More than 60 Million Stars in the Most Detailed Photo of the Milky Way Ever Taken
items.content:
Scan More than 60 Million Stars in the Most Detailed Photo of the Milky Way Ever Taken

June 30, 2026
PhotographyScience
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

In March 2025, the Euclid mission led by the The European Space Agency (ESA) enabled scientists to capture the highest resolution image ever taken of the dense, glowing center of the Milky Way galaxy. An enormous swarm of stars forms a bulge at the heart of the spiral, and researchers continue to search amid these billions of gaseous orbs for exoplanets, or any planet that’s located outside of our solar system.

“The galactic bulge—the central region of our galaxy—is a vast, tightly packed structure filled mainly with old, cooler stars, giving it its characteristic yellow colour,” ESA says. The photograph, which is taken with visible light, allows scientists to pinpoint exoplanets and measure their mass by monitoring tiny changes in starlight over time in a process called microlensing.

ESA’s Euclid image captures more than 60 million stars, plus other phenomena such as nebulae, bright star clusters, and molecular clouds that appear like amorphous, dark splotches in front of the brighter areas. Incidentally, to the human eye, they serve as a visual guide or cue to the incredible depth of field the image has actually captured.

“For comparison, Euclid’s sharpness and sensitivity in visible light is similar to the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope’s wide field camera,” ESA says. “But each pointing that Euclid captures in a few hours spans an area 270 times larger than Hubble’s field of view. To observe the same Euclid mosaic, the Keck Observatory would need around 2,000 hours.”

Zoom in on the Galactic Bulge Survey image on ESASky.

items.title: Derrick Lin Plays with Light and Scale in Emotive Photos of Miniature Dioramas
items.content:
Derrick Lin Plays with Light and Scale in Emotive Photos of Miniature Dioramas

June 29, 2026
CraftPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

A figure carrying a small suitcase crosses the gangplank onto an ocean liner. A woman stands amid a city street, waiting for a tram. And a man in a fedora heads toward historic steps in what is perhaps a European city. Yet if you look a little closer, you’ll see the roofs resemble milk cartons. The tram rolls in amid books stood on end. And in the distance beyond the docked ships… a giant coffee mug?

Since 2013, Derrick Lin has created miniature dioramas on his desk. Hand-painted figures inhabit settings constructed from cardboard and found objects, often with a nostalgic twist. And in a nod to the the tableaux’s tiny characteristics, he playfully pops in references to the scale of the real world, hence the giant writing utensils and the ceramic mug that occasionally towers architectonically in the background.

Over time, Lin has tapped into a range of emotions and experiences from stress and loneliness in urban situations to the wonder of world exploration, the passing of time, grief, and more. Through cinematic lighting and figures that often look away from the viewer, we’re transported into their experiences and encouraged by curiosity.

“I believe the thoughts and feelings we keep to ourselves are what truly shape us,” Lin says. “By using miniature figures as a manifestation of those quiet thoughts and emotions I hesitate to express, I can magnify and spotlight those emotions.”

See more on Lin’s Instagram.

items.title: In a New 223-Megapixel Image, NASA Captures 16.5 Million Stars of the Cigar Galaxy
items.content:
In a New 223-Megapixel Image, NASA Captures 16.5 Million Stars of the Cigar Galaxy

June 26, 2026
PhotographyScience
Grace Ebert
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope is back with another stunner: a new 223-megapixel composite featuring about 16.5 million stars that have been evolving over several million years. Captured by Webb’s NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) across 65 hours, the enormous image features Messier 82, also known as the Cigar galaxy, which is located 12 million light-years away.

“M82 is a mess, but it’s a beautiful mess,” said NASA fellow Adam Smercina. “We don’t fully understand what’s going on, especially concerning its evolutionary history. What could have triggered such an elevated rate of star formation? How long has this galaxy been driving plumes of material away from its center?”

Initial speculation includes a galaxy merger causing rapid star formation 10 times faster than that of the Milky Way and lasting a few hundred million years, which researchers describe as “a short-lived event in astronomical terms.” Although we can see many of these stellar objects as blue granules, there are likely many more invisible to us.

Hubble had previously looked at the galaxy, but the technology was unable to capture the same detail as Webb. As shown in a side-by-side comparison, Hubble captures many of the dust grains and ionized hydrogen gas depicted in red, orange, and yellow, while Webb highlights the staggering density of stars.

“Galaxies are such intricate ecosystems that if you truly want to understand them, you have to pull datasets from different missions together,” said Kristen McQuinn, of the Space Telescope Science Institute. “One mission cannot fully answer all of the questions we have about M82. Combining the data collected by different telescopes, like Webb and Hubble, is powerful. When you marry the datasets, you expand what you can probe, and the questions that you can pose are even more complex.”

items.title: Magnum Book Club: And They Laughed at Me
Elliot McGucken Suspends Einstein’s ‘Light Cones’ Over Desert Expanses
items.content:
Elliot McGucken Suspends Einstein’s ‘Light Cones’ Over Desert Expanses

June 23, 2026
NaturePhotographyScience
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Albert Einstein once said that “the most beautiful experience we can have is the mysterious. It is the fundamental emotion that stands at the cradle of true art and true science.” For Dr. Elliot McGucken, the sublime enigmas of nature form the basis of his explorations of landscape and light.

McGucken traverses North America’s most beautiful and striking terrain, including Death Valley where he captured a wildflower superbloom earlier this year. He revels in all kinds of natural phenomena, from the vicissitudes of the Rocky Mountains to brown bears fishing in Alaska’s Katmai National Park and Preserve to the ghostly, flood-carved walls of Antelope Canyon. He also happens to be a physicist whose research focuses on an artificial retina prosthesis that can help restore sight to those who are blind.

Although photography and physics may seem at first blush to be a world apart, they intersect in many ways, especially through the use of advanced lenses that manipulate light to create images. In this way, McGucken channels a limitless fascination with perception and seeing in which scientific inquiry drives his photography as much as the aesthetic and technical qualities of the medium. He’s also really into Albert Einstein’s Theory of Relativity and quantum mechanics, and that’s where an ongoing series called Spacetime Light Cone Sculptures dx4/dt=ic comes in.

McGucken delves specifically into the study of the fourth dimension, drawing on Einstein’s 1922 book The Meaning of Relativity, in which the renowned scientist illustrated a “light cone” that represented “the deep, physical relationship between space, time, and the velocity of light,” McGucken says. This almost hourglass-like shape, with two cones that meet at their tips, forms the basis of Spacetime Light Cone Sculptures dx4/dt=ic.

McGucken describes the works as “sculptures upon nature’s exalted easel,” utilizing contemporary technology to illuminate theories of existence and the cosmos. He sends a drone into the air over dramatic and remote Southwest landscapes to capture long exposures of conical spirals of light. Over the years, he’s visited the Trona Pinnacles in the California Desert Conservation Area and the Mobius Arch rock formation in the Alabama Hills, among other places.

See more on the artist’s Instagram and purchase prints on his website. You might also enjoy Rueben Wu’s glowing light paintings.

items.title: Construct Your Own Miniature Paper Brutalist Circuses with ‘Cirk’
items.content:
Construct Your Own Miniature Paper Brutalist Circuses with ‘Cirk’

June 23, 2026
BooksDesignHistoryPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

When we think of traveling circuses, the “big top” tent likely springs to mind with its acrobats, clowns, tightrope walkers, and other entertainers and pageantry. Sometimes the traditions are controversial, such as the use of elephants and lions for performances. But visions of bedazzled animals or the swinging trapeze are nevertheless etched in our collective memory.

In the former U.S.S.R., the tradition took on a whole new meaning. Circuses had been nationalized in 1919, a few years before the Soviet Union was formed. Along with theater, opera, and music, the genre was also co-opted by the socialist government as a propaganda machine, turning family-friendly entertainment into a channel for Communist Party ideological messages. And with its enormous popularity, venues were in demand.

Between the 1950s and 1980s, the U.S.S.R. commissioned dozens of arenas across the nation, conceived as year-round event venues. Their strikingly geometric, brutalist designs are eye-catching and modern, reflecting the government’s fixation on expressing its power and technological progress. In the 1960s, the Space Race exemplified the Soviet Union’s critical role on the world stage. Arena architecture was yet another way to demonstrate the nation’s might, even occasionally resembling flying saucers.

Cirk, a new book from David Navarro and Martyna Sobecka of Zupagrafika, highlights the wide range of permanent circuses still standing around Eastern Europe, Central Asia, and further afield. “These arenas combined socialist modernism, experimental engineering, and choreographed spectacle,” the publisher says, adding: “Together, they reveal a lesser-known chapter of postwar modernist architecture shaped by ideology and mass entertainment.”

One of Cirk‘s more playful features is a series of pop-out paper models of actual buildings including state circus buildings in Bishkek, Chișinău, Dnipro, Moscow, and Tashkent. Find your copy on Zupagrafika’s website.

Joe Kennedy is a photographer based in Sydney, Australia. Humble, hard working with an innate curiosity that often leads him on unpredictable adventures. Joe is a photographer that strives to create images brimming with narrative and meaning. Much of his work is observational in nature, recording people and places through a lense that combines art and straight documentary coverage. This stems from his working class sensibilities where photography was always seen as a way to record people, places and events rather than an art. He is influenced deeply by Australian landscape and culture from the colour palettes he employs to the subject matter he chooses to capture. As such, much of his personal work strives to tell uncovered or overlooked stories of people and communities of regional Australia.

items.title: Tamara Dean Blurs the Boundary Between Bodies and Natural Landscapes
items.content:
Tamara Dean Blurs the Boundary Between Bodies and Natural Landscapes

June 15, 2026
NaturePhotography
Jackie Andres
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

Based in the foothills of Cambewarra Mountain in New South Wales, Australia, Tamara Dean captures ethereal images that explore the intrinsic bond between the human body and the natural world. She is driven by what she describes as a desire to “explore the reality that humans are not separate from nature, but intrinsically part of it.”

Using bodies to express this relationship, the figures within her compositions do not emerge as prominent subjects of portraiture. Instead, they exist as elements embedded within each scene, often emerging as extensions of surrounding flora. “I am interested in those moments when the body appears to merge with the landscape, becoming almost plant-like, animal-like or elemental, suggesting that we are participants in nature rather than observers of it,” she explains.

“Introversion” depicts crouching figures hiding inside frilly blue tutus that imitate their neighboring flowers, calling to an almost instinctive impulse to camouflage. In a vibrant pop of color, two hot pink-haired heads in “In Bloom” mimic nearby lotus flower buds, waiting to bloom alongside lotus plants.

Gesture is an integral part of Dean’s process. While directing the figures within her work, the photographer explains, “I often encourage them to respond intuitively to their surroundings. At times, this involves reflecting the structures, rhythms, or symmetries found in nearby flora and foliage through their physical placement, posture, or gesture.” These visible idiosyncrasies further the dynamic exchange between human and other life forms.

Lately, Dean has spent more time painting. “It’s something I have always done quietly in the background as part of my creative process,” she explains. “But only now that my children are 19 and 20 have I been able to dedicate myself to it more fully. I’m enjoying the challenge of working in a different medium and the change in perspective it brings.”

These paintings, alongside several photographs, will be included in a forthcoming solo exhibition early next year at Michael Reid in Sydney. Last week, she opened Leave only footprints at Manly Art Gallery and Museum, which is on view through August 2. Find Dean on Instagram to follow along with her ongoing interdisciplinary explorations.

‘Women in Trees’ Celebrates a Quirky Collection of Anonymous Snapshots
items.content:
‘Women in Trees’ Celebrates a Quirky Collection of Anonymous Snapshots

June 11, 2026
BooksHistoryPhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

As collector Jochen Raiß (1969-2022) scoured flea markets and antique stalls for the better part of three decades for snapshots, he began to notice a running theme. Over time, he amassed a trove of photos by anonymous photographers with an unusually high number of portraits of women posing in trees. Swiss newspaper Züricher Tagesanzeiger asked, “What are they all doing up there?” And German paper Der Spiegel posited that the arbor-climbing might be a “forgotten popular sport.” Whatever the reason, the mystery is nearly as fun as the photos.

A hardcover edition of Women in Trees from Hatje Cantz, published in German and English, follows two titles published in 2016 and 2017 that celebrate these quirky images. Find your copy on the publisher’s website.

items.title: Natural Dyes Merge with Mixed Media in Annalise Neil’s Dreamy Cyanotypes
items.content:
Natural Dyes Merge with Mixed Media in Annalise Neil’s Dreamy Cyanotypes

June 11, 2026
ArtNaturePhotography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

“Matter is memory, and memory is a medium,” says artist Annalise Neil, whose surreal cyanotypes brim with animals, fungi, geological specimens, shells, and more that she augments with watercolor. Recently, the artist has been adding rich, earthy tones with natural dyes such as wild strawberry leaf, oak gall, loquat leaf, and chestnut. She has used botanical teas to shift the natural blue color of the cyanotypes for quite a while, but the sepia tonality has emerged as a larger focus lately, which allows her to layer hues like browns and purples.

Neil’s experiences in nature profoundly influence her individual pieces in a process that she poetically describes as “melting, rolling, pinching, sanding, walking across meadows, cheek on sun-warmed boulders.” This year, she’s a resident artist at Volcan Mountain Foundation in Julian, California, which merges artistic and scientific inquiry. “I endeavor to create work that will lead to contemplation and reflection and that invites a thoughtful examination of our relationship to reality and our surroundings,” she says.

“For my site-specific work, I begin by hiking for many days and photographing intriguing things I find, including birds and mammals, plants, geological forms, and insects,” she says. “As I photograph specimens in wild and cultivated spaces, I capture a brief version of their existence that I transmute into a negative and then into a cyanotype.” The images are then supported on hand-carved wooden panels.

Neil’s work is currently on view in shows in San Diego: Unfold Projects Exhibition 01: We Must Imagine It, presented in collaboration with ICA San Diego and continuing through August 2, and Organica: Flora to Fauna at The Granger Hotel in San Diego, curated by JFIN Collective, which continues through the end of the year. See more and follow updates on the artist’s Instagram.

items.title: Brendon Burton’s Enigmatic Photographs Preserve Traces of North American Life
items.content:
Brendon Burton’s Enigmatic Photographs Preserve Traces of North American Life

June 10, 2026
Photography
Jackie Andres
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

As Brendon Burton continues to pursue the strange corners of rural North America, the Portland-based photographer has discovered a newfound interest in the people who once inhabited them.

No longer entirely devoid of human figures, his isolated landscapes step into the walls of abandoned homes and provide a setting for enigmatic narratives. Burton’s quiet introduction to life through the presence of domestic, intimate objects allows the viewer to piece together a speculative story about their previous owners.

From a pair of worn boots and aged portraits to a patterned quilt resting upon a bed that was once made for the last time, photography introduces an element of permanence, preserving existence while original context has long faded away.

Burton has turned to direction and video of late, working on five music videos slated to release within the next few months. He has also published a second edition of his book, Epitaph, which you can pick up on his website. Follow Burton on Instagram to tag along on his travels and adventures.

items.excerpt: Kristoﬀer Axén (b. 1984, Stockholm) is a contemporary visual artist working across painting and photography. His practice explores atmosphere, memory, and the tension between revelation and erasure, producing works that hover between figuration and abstraction. Rec
items.content:
Kristoﬀer Axén (b. 1984, Stockholm) is a contemporary visual artist working across painting and photography. His practice explores atmosphere, memory, and the tension between revelation and erasure, producing works that hover between figuration and abstraction.

Recent highlights include a solo presentation at the 2024 InCadaqués International Festival (Spain), recognition in the OD Photo Prize 2024 (Judges’ Picks), a major group exhibition at Galerie Hors Champs, Paris (Winter 2024 / January 2025), and participation in Pedigree at OHSH Projects, London (2025). In 2025 his work was exhibited at Photo London, where he was shortlisted for the Nikon Emerging Photographer Award and written about in The Guardian. His work was also published in the Fresh Eyes 2025 book of emerging European photography.

Looking ahead, his work will appear in an upcoming Netflix production (Fall 2026). Earlier in his career, Axén was awarded the 2011 Tierney Fellowship in New York and selected for reGeneration2: Tomorrow’s Photographers Today (2010), a Musée de l’Elysée traveling exhibition presented in over a dozen countries. He has held solo exhibitions in New York (Munch Gallery), Copenhagen (Galerie Pi), and Stockholm (Gallery Domeij), and participated in major group shows including Liljevalchs Vårsalong (Stockholm), Aperture Gallery (New York), and Musée de l’Elysée (Lausanne).

His works are held in private and public collections including the ICP Collection (New York), Michaelis School of Fine Arts (Cape Town), and MONA (Tasmania). He has been featured in Frieze, The Guardian, British Journal of Photography, The New York Times, and Vogue Italia, among others.

He lives and works in Stockholm, Sweden.

items.title: Dave Krugman’s ‘WINDOWS’ Captures a Multitudinous Portrait of New York City
items.content:
Dave Krugman’s ‘WINDOWS’ Captures a Multitudinous Portrait of New York City

June 8, 2026
Photography
Kate Mothes
  • Share
  • Pin
  • Email

As Dave Krugman traverses the streets of New York City, camera in hand, he seeks patterns. Throughout his wide-ranging practice spanning portraits, automobiles, tourism, and more, he studies “humanity’s intersection with cities and how people are influenced by their immediate environment,” says a statement. Whether in the countryside or the middle of an urban hub, rhythms and typologies emerge.

The Brooklyn-based photographer began documenting windows throughout New York City several years ago, and his aptly named series compiles a cross-section of his captures over the past half decade. Taken at night, these virtually infinite portals into individual lives are illuminated from within. Krugman focuses only on the light, shadow, and things placed just inside, such as cat beds, curtains, and holiday decorations that anyone can see as they pass by on the street. Each window on its own is a curiosity; arranged in a grid, they comprise a medley and a kind of portrait of the city.

“New York, despite being so densely populated, can often be a lonely place,” Krugman says. “By documenting the individuality and variation of these windows, and then sequencing them into randomized grids, we’re able to recreate the sense of belonging and sonder that one feels while wandering the storied streets of this beautiful metropolis.”

Leaning into the concept of “sonder,” which is an awareness of the immense complexity of others’ lives in addition to our own, the artist nudges our recognition of the unique experiences of the people behind these windows. “To me, WINDOWS is a reflection about how our similarities to each other overpower our differences, and how our isolation is ultimately overwhelmed by our sense of community and togetherness,” he says.

The search for patterns continues to inspire Krugman on wanderings throughout New York City. He likens the experience to foraging or collecting seashells on the coast. “That excitement and surprise of the variance and ‘success’ of finding a ‘good one’ is rooted in our deepest evolutionary instincts,” he says. “Layering that tendency over the built world, which often feels more foreign and unnatural, helps to remind me that we are still an extension of that natural world—still a part of it—even if this particular forest is one of steel, stone, and glass.”

Krugman is currently organizing a project to be released in two phases, including a digital art sale with Transient Labs and a physical print sale. Updates will be released via his newsletter. Krugman is also the founder of ALLSHIPS, which he describes as “a culture company” for artists. See more on his Instagram.
